questions.stem: What are the three roles of the WTO?
options: Administering trade rules, providing a forum for negotiation, and settling disputes
Setting the tariff rates that all members must apply
Lending to countries in balance of payments difficulty
Fixing exchange rates between member currencies
questions.why: Members set their own tariffs within the agreed rules; the WTO administers those rules.
whyNot: Members set their own tariffs.
That is the IMF's role.
Exchange rates are outside its remit.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: A customs union applies a common external tariff to non-members
A customs union allows free movement of labour
A customs union shares a single currency
A free trade area retains internal tariffs
questions.why: The common external tariff also removes the rules-of-origin problem and removes members' freedom to set their own trade policy.
whyNot: That comes with a common market.
That comes with a monetary union.
Both remove internal tariffs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a common market?
options: A customs union that also allows free movement of goods, services, capital and labour
A free trade area with harmonised tax rates
A group of countries sharing one currency
A market in which all firms charge the same price
questions.why: Its economic significance is that factors move to where their return is highest, raising allocative efficiency across the bloc.
whyNot: Tax harmonisation is not the defining feature.
That is a monetary union.
That is not a form of economic integration.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the most favoured nation principle?
options: A WTO member must extend the same trade terms to all members
A member must give its best terms to the poorest members only
A member must charge its lowest tariff on all imports
A member must trade most with its nearest neighbour
questions.why: Regional blocs are permitted as an exception to it, which is the source of the tension between blocs and the WTO.
whyNot: It applies to all members equally.
It requires equal treatment, not a particular rate.
It says nothing about geography.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines trade creation?
options: Trade shifting from higher-cost domestic production to lower-cost production within the bloc
Trade shifting from an efficient non-member to a less efficient member
The total increase in a bloc's trade with the rest of the world
The creation of new export products by bloc members
questions.why: It is a genuine efficiency gain, because resources are used where they are most productive.
whyNot: That is trade diversion.
Blocs typically divert trade away from non-members.
That is product development.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines trade diversion?
options: Trade shifting from a more efficient non-member to a less efficient member because of the external tariff
Trade shifting from goods to services
Trade being rerouted through a third country to avoid duty
Trade falling during a recession
questions.why: It is an efficiency loss, and the imported good costs more in real terms than it need.
whyNot: That is a change in trade composition.
That is transhipment.
That is cyclical.

questions.stem: Under what conditions is a bloc more likely to raise welfare?
options: When members are already substantial trading partners and the external tariff is low
When members produce identical goods and the external tariff is high
When members have no existing trade with each other
When the bloc has as many members as possible
questions.why: Trade creation is then more likely to exceed trade diversion, which is the central welfare test.
whyNot: A high external tariff maximises diversion.
Little existing trade means little scope for creation.
Size alone does not determine the balance of the two effects.

questions.stem: Why are rules of origin needed in a free trade area but not a customs union?
options: Members keep their own external tariffs, so goods could enter through the lowest-tariff member
Customs unions do not trade with non-members
Free trade areas prohibit imports from non-members
Customs unions have no internal tariffs
questions.why: The common external tariff removes the incentive, and with it the paperwork, which is a real cost saving.
whyNot: Customs unions trade with non-members under the common tariff.
They permit such imports, subject to each member's own tariff.
Free trade areas also have no internal tariffs.

questions.stem: What does a member give up by joining an economic and monetary union?
options: An independent monetary policy and the ability to let the exchange rate adjust
The ability to trade with non-members
Control of its own public spending entirely
The right to set its own product standards only
questions.why: Whether that is acceptable depends on how similar members' economic cycles are, which is the optimal currency area question.
whyNot: External trade continues under the common tariff.
Fiscal policy generally remains national, subject to coordination.
Standards are harmonised at the common market stage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the least glamorous and most substantial benefit of bloc membership for small firms?
options: Lower transaction costs from fewer customs procedures and one set of standards
The ability to charge higher prices
Protection from competitors within the bloc
Guaranteed access to government contracts
questions.why: The fixed cost of compliance is proportionally largest for small firms, so removing it matters most to them.
whyNot: Greater competition tends to lower prices.
Barriers to members are removed, not raised.
Procurement access varies by agreement.

questions.stem: Why can free movement of factors create problems as well as benefits?
options: Emigration from poorer members can amount to a brain drain and immigration pressures services
Factors of production cannot physically move between countries
It always reduces total output in the bloc
It requires a single currency to operate
questions.why: Efficiency rises as factors move to their highest return, and the distributional effects between members are uneven.
whyNot: Free movement is precisely designed to allow it.
It raises allocative efficiency and total output.
It operates at the common market stage without a shared currency.

questions.stem: Why are blocs in tension with the most favoured nation principle?
options: They offer members better terms than non-members, which is discrimination
They require members to raise tariffs on each other
They prevent members from joining the WTO
They set exchange rates for their members
questions.why: The WTO permits them as an exception, on condition that they cover substantially all trade and do not raise barriers against non-members.
whyNot: Internal tariffs are removed.
Bloc members are WTO members.
Exchange rates are a separate matter.

questions.stem: What is meant by asking whether blocs are building blocks or stumbling blocks?
options: Whether they lead towards wider global liberalisation or substitute for it
Whether they are made of customs unions or free trade areas
Whether they raise or lower members' tariffs on each other
Whether they are permitted under WTO rules
questions.why: Blocs liberalise faster and deeper than the WTO has managed, and preferential regional access reduces the incentive to pursue global liberalisation.
whyNot: It is not about their structure.
Internal tariffs fall in every type of bloc.
They are permitted as an exception.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the WTO?
options: Agriculture and services remained far less liberalised than manufactures
It has no developing country members
It cannot settle any disputes
It sets no rules at all
questions.why: That disadvantages developing countries whose comparative advantage is often agricultural.
whyNot: Most of its members are developing countries.
Dispute settlement is one of its three core roles.
It administers an extensive body of rules.

questions.stem: Which group bears the cost of trade diversion?
options: Non-members, particularly developing countries excluded from major blocs
Only the bloc's own consumers
Only the bloc's producers
Nobody, because diversion is a pure gain
questions.why: Bloc consumers also pay more than they need for diverted imports, and the excluded exporters lose the market entirely.
whyNot: Consumers bear part of it, and excluded exporters bear the rest.
Producers within the bloc gain from diversion.
It is an efficiency loss, not a gain.

questions.stem: What further information would most improve an answer on whether a country benefits from bloc membership?
options: The share of the country's trade already conducted with bloc members
The population of each member state
The number of years the bloc has existed
The languages spoken in the bloc
questions.why: Existing trade with members determines how much scope there is for trade creation rather than diversion.
whyNot: Population alone does not determine the welfare effect.
Age of the bloc is not the relevant variable.
Language is not an economic determinant here.
